title: Vietnam
hookLine: where Theravada and Mahayana meet, and Chan becomes Thien

lines: SAFFRON ROBES IN THE MEKONG DELTA.
cards: Two temples, one country. In the Mekong Delta, in the far south of Vietnam, monks in saffron robes chant in Pali under steep, gilded Khmer roofs.

A long way north, in a pagoda near Hanoi, a nun in brown robes sits in silent meditation, and an hour later the same hall fills with lay people chanting the name of Amitabha Buddha, a Mahayana practice.

Different robes, different languages, different streams of the teaching. Across Southeast Asia, both streams have shown up in stone: Theravada in Sri Lanka, Myanmar and Thailand, Mahayana at Angkor and Borobudur.
In Vietnam, they live side by side today.

teach.h: MAHAYANA AND THERAVADA, BOTH AT HOME.
teach.b: First, the two streams. Mahayana Buddhism came into Vietnam with texts written in Chinese characters, and it shaped pagodas and monasteries across the country.
Theravada lives on too, especially among the Khmer communities of the south, with Pali chanting and saffron robes, and some Vietnamese monasteries follow it as well. Second, Chan becomes Thien.

teach.h: CHAN IN CHINA, THIEN IN VIETNAM.
teach.b: One Mahayana school, called Chan in China and Zen in Japan, is called Thien in Vietnam. Its heart is meditation: sitting, seeing clearly, not relying on words alone.
Tradition says all three names come from the old Indian word for meditation, dhyana. Third, a king on a mountain.

teach.h: A KING WHO BECAME A MONK.
teach.b: Vietnamese tradition remembers a king named Tran Nhan Tong, who gave up his throne, became a monk, and went to live on Yen Tu mountain.
The Thien school linked to him is called Truc Lam, the Bamboo Grove, and it's still practiced today. Fourth, both in one hall.
In Vietnamese pagodas, Thien meditation and Pure Land chanting live side by side, sometimes on the same day, with the same people, who don't treat it as a choice they must make.

And beneath both streams is shared ground. The Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation, puts it in one line: "Not to commit any sin, to do good, and to purify one's mind, that is the teaching of (all) the Awakened."
A Khmer monk in the delta and a Thien nun near Hanoi could both say that line and mean it.

how: In Vietnamese pagodas, monks, nuns and lay Buddhists practice Thien meditation and also chant the name of Amitabha Buddha, while Khmer Theravada temples in the south keep Pali chanting and the morning alms.

games.q: you're a lay Buddhist at a pagoda near Hanoi. the morning has silent Thien meditation; the evening has chanting of Amitabha's name. what do people there do?
o: pick one practice and stay away from the other.
join both, meditation and chanting side by side.
keep meditation for monks and chanting for lay people.
games.why: in Vietnamese pagodas, Thien meditation and Pure Land chanting live side by side, and the same people can join both.

practice: Think of a place in your own life where two ways live together, two languages in one kitchen, two family traditions at one holiday table, a morning person and a night owl under one roof.
Notice where the two rub against each other and where they've quietly made room, and let both be there, side by side, without judging which is right.
